claim: The balance between Th17 and T regulatory (Treg) cells critically modulates immune homeostasis.
source: The balance between Th17 and T regulatory (Treg) cells critically modulates immune homeostasis, with an inadequate Treg response contributing to inflammatory disease.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract that represents established scientific understanding in the field.

claim: An inadequate Treg response contributes to inflammatory disease.
source: The balance between Th17 and T regulatory (Treg) cells critically modulates immune homeostasis, with an inadequate Treg response contributing to inflammatory disease.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: DYRK1A regulates the balance between Th17 and Treg cells.
source: Using an unbiased chemical biology approach, we identified a novel role for the dual specificity tyrosine-phosphorylation-regulated kinase DYRK1A in regulating this balance.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study stated in the abstract.

claim: Inhibition of DYRK1A enhances Treg differentiation.
source: Inhibition of DYRK1A enhances Treg differentiation and impairs Th17 differentiation without affecting known pathways of Treg/Th17 differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Inhibition of DYRK1A impairs Th17 differentiation.
source: Inhibition of DYRK1A enhances Treg differentiation and impairs Th17 differentiation without affecting known pathways of Treg/Th17 differentiation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data.

claim: DYRK1A inhibition does not affect known pathways of Treg/Th17 differentiation.
source: Inhibition of DYRK1A enhances Treg differentiation and impairs Th17 differentiation without affecting known pathways of Treg/Th17 differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing no effects on mTOR, SMAD2/3, or STAT3/RORγT pathways.

claim: DYRK1A represents a novel mechanistic node at the branch point between commitment to either Treg or Th17 lineages.
source: Thus, DYRK1A represents a novel mechanistic node at the branch point between commitment to either Treg or Th17 lineages.
evidence: This is an interpretive conclusion based on the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Treg cells generated using the DYRK1A inhibitor harmine potently attenuate inflammation in multiple experimental models of systemic autoimmunity and mucosal inflammation.
source: Importantly, both Treg cells generated using the DYRK1A inhibitor harmine and direct administration of harmine itself potently attenuate inflammation in multiple experimental models of systemic autoimmunity and mucosal inflammation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by in vivo experimental data.

claim: Direct administration of harmine potently attenuates inflammation in multiple experimental models of systemic autoimmunity and mucosal inflammation.
source: Importantly, both Treg cells generated using the DYRK1A inhibitor harmine and direct administration of harmine itself potently attenuate inflammation in multiple experimental models of systemic autoimmunity and mucosal inflammation.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by in vivo experimental data.

claim: DYRK1A is a physiologically relevant regulator of Treg cell differentiation.
source: Our results identify DYRK1A as a physiologically relevant regulator of Treg cell differentiation and suggest a broader role for other DYRK family members in immune homeostasis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Other DYRK family members may have a broader role in immune homeostasis.
source: Our results identify DYRK1A as a physiologically relevant regulator of Treg cell differentiation and suggest a broader role for other DYRK family members in immune homeostasis.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the findings about DYRK1A.

claim: The appropriate and balanced differentiation of naïve CD4+ T helper cells into pro-inflammatory or anti-inflammatory subsets is an important determinant of immune homeostasis.
source: The appropriate and balanced differentiation of naïve CD4+ T helper (Th) cells into either pro-inflammatory effector subsets, such as Th1 and Th17 cells, or anti-inflammatory subsets, largely represented by regulatory T (Treg) cells, is an important determinant of immune homeostasis, dysregulation of which underlies the pathology of inflammatory diseases and cancer (Josefowicz et al., 2012; Cretney et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Dysregulation of Th cell differentiation underlies the pathology of inflammatory diseases and cancer.
source: The appropriate and balanced differentiation of naïve CD4+ T helper (Th) cells into either pro-inflammatory effector subsets, such as Th1 and Th17 cells, or anti-inflammatory subsets, largely represented by regulatory T (Treg) cells, is an important determinant of immune homeostasis, dysregulation of which underlies the pathology of inflammatory diseases and cancer (Josefowicz et al., 2012; Cretney et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Genome-wide association studies of inflammatory diseases such as type 1 diabetes and inflammatory bowel disease implicate genes important for the differentiation and function of Treg cells.
source: Genome-wide association studies of inflammatory diseases such as type 1 diabetes (T1D) and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) support this notion, implicating genes important for the differentiation and function of Treg cells (Khor et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Low-dose IL-2 has been used to enhance Treg cells and attenuate inflammation associated with graft-versus-host disease and HCV vasculitis.
source: The active translational interest in manipulating this process is exemplified by recent attempts using low-dose IL-2 to enhance Treg cells and attenuate the inflammation associated with graft-versus-host disease and HCV vasculitis (Koreth et al., 2011; Saadoun et al., 2011; von Boehmer and Daniel, 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior clinical studies.

claim: IL-2 has numerous effects, reflecting the larger issue that more targeted therapies to specifically manipulate individual Th lineages remain lacking.
source: While these results are encouraging, IL-2 has numerous effects and reflects the larger issue that more targeted therapies to specifically manipulate individual Th lineages remain lacking, due at least in part to an incomplete understanding of the pathways that contribute to Th differentiation.
evidence: This is a statement of the current state of the field based on established knowledge.

claim: More targeted therapies to specifically manipulate individual Th lineages remain lacking due to an incomplete understanding of the pathways that contribute to Th differentiation.
source: While these results are encouraging, IL-2 has numerous effects and reflects the larger issue that more targeted therapies to specifically manipulate individual Th lineages remain lacking, due at least in part to an incomplete understanding of the pathways that contribute to Th differentiation.
evidence: This is a statement of the current state of the field based on established knowledge.

claim: Commitment to the Treg cell lineage is exemplified by expression of the hallmark transcription factor FOXP3.
source: In this regard, commitment to the Treg cell lineage is exemplified by expression of the hallmark transcription factor FOXP3 and occurs in either the thymus or the periphery (Josefowicz et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: Treg cell differentiation occurs in either the thymus or the periphery.
source: In this regard, commitment to the Treg cell lineage is exemplified by expression of the hallmark transcription factor FOXP3 and occurs in either the thymus or the periphery (Josefowicz et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: TGF-β1 is the canonical cytokine that drives Treg cell differentiation.
source: The canonical cytokine that drives Treg cell differentiation is TGF-β1 and the differentiation of peripheral Treg (pTreg) cells requires TGF-β1 signaling through SMAD2 and SMAD3 (Gu et al., 2012; Josefowicz et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature and represents established knowledge.

claim: The differentiation of peripheral Treg cells requires TGF-β1 signaling through SMAD2 and SMAD3.
source: The canonical cytokine that drives Treg cell differentiation is TGF-β1 and the differentiation of peripheral Treg (pTreg) cells requires TGF-β1 signaling through SMAD2 and SMAD3 (Gu et al., 2012; Josefowicz et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: TGF-β1 plays a role in thymic Treg cell differentiation.
source: TGF-β1 also plays a role in thymic Treg (tTreg) cell differentiation, as exemplified by the significant but transient decrease in early Treg cell generation upon T cell-specific deletion of the TGF-β1 RI subunit (Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: T cell-specific deletion of the TGF-β1 RI subunit leads to a significant but transient decrease in early Treg cell generation.
source: TGF-β1 also plays a role in thymic Treg (tTreg) cell differentiation, as exemplified by the significant but transient decrease in early Treg cell generation upon T cell-specific deletion of the TGF-β1 RI subunit (Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: TGF-β1 may be more important for maintaining the pool of Treg cell precursors than instructing Foxp3 expression in the thymic compartment.
source: However, TGF-β1 may be more important for maintaining the pool of Treg cell precursors than instructing Foxp3 expression in this compartment (Josefowicz et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: TGF-β1 has not proven to be a clinically useful target to manipulate Treg cell differentiation.
source: Similarly to IL-2, TGF-β1 exerts multiple effects on different cell types and has not proven to be a clinically useful target to manipulate Treg cell differentiation, again pointing to the need to better understand the breadth of pathways involved.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of clinical applications based on established knowledge.

claim: Studies in SMAD2/3 doubly deficient mice point to TGF-β1-dependent, SMAD2/3-independent signals in tTreg cell differentiation and function.
source: In this regard, studies in SMAD2/3 doubly deficient mice point to TGF-β1-dependent, SMAD2/3-independent signals in tTreg cell differentiation and function, demonstrating the relevance of non-canonical pathways, even in the context of well-described cytokines (Gu et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Gene expression profiling has been more successful for Th17 cell differentiation than for Treg cell differentiation in identifying differentially expressed genes.
source: This approach has been more successful for Th17 cell differentiation, pointing to the transcription factors Batf, Ahr and Ikzf3 and the sodium chloride sensor Sgk1 (Veldhoen et al., 2008; Schraml et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2013), than for Treg cell differentiation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Gene expression profiling has identified Batf, Ahr, Ikzf3, and Sgk1 as important for Th17 cell differentiation.
source: This approach has been more successful for Th17 cell differentiation, pointing to the transcription factors Batf, Ahr and Ikzf3 and the sodium chloride sensor Sgk1 (Veldhoen et al., 2008; Schraml et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2013), than for Treg cell differentiation.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Mutations in STAT3 can lead to hyper-IgE syndrome.
source: For example, the finding that mutations in STAT3 (which transduces signals from IL-6, a canonical Th17 cytokine) can lead to hyper-IgE syndrome (HIES) led to the discovery that this subset of HIES patients fail to generate Th17 cells, potentially accounting for their susceptibility to fungal infection (Ma et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: HIES patients with STAT3 mutations fail to generate Th17 cells.
source: For example, the finding that mutations in STAT3 (which transduces signals from IL-6, a canonical Th17 cytokine) can lead to hyper-IgE syndrome (HIES) led to the discovery that this subset of HIES patients fail to generate Th17 cells, potentially accounting for their susceptibility to fungal infection (Ma et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The failure to generate Th17 cells in HIES patients with STAT3 mutations potentially accounts for their susceptibility to fungal infection.
source: For example, the finding that mutations in STAT3 (which transduces signals from IL-6, a canonical Th17 cytokine) can lead to hyper-IgE syndrome (HIES) led to the discovery that this subset of HIES patients fail to generate Th17 cells, potentially accounting for their susceptibility to fungal infection (Ma et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature and involves inference about disease mechanism.

claim: SGK1 regulates Th17 cell differentiation.
source: There are also therapeutic implications; for instance, the discovery that SGK1 regulates Th17 cell differentiation led to the hypothesis that increased dietary salt intake may contribute to increased risk of autoimmune disease (Kleinewietfeld et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The discovery that SGK1 regulates Th17 cell differentiation led to the hypothesis that increased dietary salt intake may contribute to increased risk of autoimmune disease.
source: There are also therapeutic implications; for instance, the discovery that SGK1 regulates Th17 cell differentiation led to the hypothesis that increased dietary salt intake may contribute to increased risk of autoimmune disease (Kleinewietfeld et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Analyses of over 100 gene expression profiles of various CD4+ subsets led to the discovery of novel transcription factors, including Lef1 and Gata1, that regulate Treg cell differentiation.
source: Analyses of over 100 gene expression profiles of various CD4+ subsets led to the discovery of novel transcription factors, including Lef1 and Gata1, that regulate Treg cell differentiation and a model of how they cooperate to establish the Treg cell transcription profile (Fu et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Zbtb25 is a transcription factor predominantly expressed in T cells that represses NFAT signaling in response to T cell receptor engagement.
source: In another example, the compilation of 557 publicly available microarrays covering over 100 tissues and primary cells facilitated the discovery of Zbtb25 as a transcription factor predominantly expressed in T cells that represses NFAT signaling in response to T cell receptor engagement (Benita et al., 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Defects in autophagy have been associated with IBD.
source: In this regard, defects in autophagy have been associated with IBD.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Some autophagy-enhancing compounds specifically inhibit Th17 cell differentiation while another subset specifically enhances Treg cell differentiation.
source: Efforts to find compounds that enhance autophagy led to the observation that some autophagy-enhancing compounds specifically inhibit Th17 cell differentiation while another subset specifically enhances Treg cell differentiation, suggesting that these compounds highlight targets which modulate distinct sets of disease-relevant pathways (Shaw et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Mechanistic studies of all-trans retinoic acid and rapamycin pointed to roles for RAR-α and mTOR signaling in Treg cell differentiation respectively.
source: For example, mechanistic studies of all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) and rapamycin, two well-studied Treg cell enhancers, pointed to roles for RAR-α and mTOR signaling in Treg cell differentiation respectively (Coombes et al., 2007; Mucida et al., 2007; Sun et al., 2007; Haxhinasto et al., 2008; Hill et al., 2008; Sauer et al., 2008; Hall et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: The microbial metabolites proprionate and butyrate enhance Treg cell differentiation.
source: More recently, the discovery of the microbial metabolites proprionate and butyrate as enhancers of Treg cell differentiation, amongst other effects, have highlighted roles for the short-chain fatty acid receptor GPR43 and histone deacetylases in Treg cell differentiation (Arpaia et al., 2013; Furusawa et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The discovery of proprionate and butyrate as Treg cell enhancers highlighted roles for GPR43 and histone deacetylases in Treg cell differentiation.
source: More recently, the discovery of the microbial metabolites proprionate and butyrate as enhancers of Treg cell differentiation, amongst other effects, have highlighted roles for the short-chain fatty acid receptor GPR43 and histone deacetylases in Treg cell differentiation (Arpaia et al., 2013; Furusawa et al., 2013; Smith et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Primary murine CD4+ T cells were reproducibly differentiated into Treg, Th1 or Th17 lineages in a manner dependent upon the concentration of TGF-β1, IL-12 or IL-6 and/or IL-1β respectively.
source: Primary murine CD4+ T cells were reproducibly differentiated into Treg, Th1 or Th17 lineages in a manner dependent upon the concentration of TGF-β1, IL-12 or IL-6 and/or IL-1β respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Lineage commitment was determined using flow cytometric detection of FOXP3, IFNγ and/or IL-17.
source: Lineage commitment was determined using the gold standard of flow cytometric detection of FOXP3, IFNγ and/or IL-17.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental approach.

claim: The study screened 3281 compounds comprising FDA-approved drugs and tool compounds with known mechanisms.
source: To find small molecules that enhance Treg cell differentiation, Treglow conditions were used to screen 3281 compounds comprising FDA-approved drugs and tool compounds with known mechanisms (Shaw et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental approach.

claim: There is a negative correlation between the number of live cells in culture and the percentage of FOXP3+ cells in Treglow conditions.
source: Our studies revealed a previously unreported negative correlation between the number of live cells in culture and the percentage of FOXP3+ cells in Treglow conditions, not observed in Treghi, Th1low/hi or Th17low/hi conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The negative correlation between live cells and FOXP3+ cells is not observed in Treghi, Th1low/hi or Th17low/hi conditions.
source: Our studies revealed a previously unreported negative correlation between the number of live cells in culture and the percentage of FOXP3+ cells in Treglow conditions, not observed in Treghi, Th1low/hi or Th17low/hi conditions (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The screen recovered numerous compounds previously reported to enhance Treg cell differentiation, including statins, artemisinin, and retinoic acids.
source: Numerous compounds previously reported to enhance Treg cell differentiation were recovered, including the hypolipidemic statins (lovastatin and simvastatin), artemisinin and ATRA as well as related retinoic acids (9-cis retinoic acid and 13-cis retinoic acid), validating our experimental approach (Coombes et al., 2007; Mucida et al., 2007; Sun et al., 2007; Kagami et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from the study that validates the experimental approach by recovering known compounds, supported by citations.

claim: The study identified 14 compounds hitherto unreported to specifically enhance differentiation of Treg, but neither Th1 nor Th17, cells.
source: We identified 14 compounds hitherto unreported to specifically enhance differentiation of Treg, but neither Th1 nor Th17, cells (Figure 1B,C and Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by data shown in the figures.

claim: Only rapamycin significantly inhibited S6 phosphorylation among all 21 Treg cell enhancers tested.
source: Only rapamycin, the positive control, significantly inhibited S6 phosphorylation (1-way ANOVA with Dunnett correction, threshold p < 0.05).
evidence: This is a finding from the study based on experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: All 14 novel Treg cell enhancers appear to work independently of mTOR.
source: Thus, all 14 novel Treg cell enhancers appear to work independently of mTOR and potentially point to undiscovered mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the S6 phosphorylation data.

claim: Th17 cell differentiation was typically more inhibited (≥40%) than Th1 by the Treg cell enhancers.
source: Th17 cell differentiation was typically more inhibited (≥40%) than Th1, likely related to Treg cells and Th17 cells arising from a common progenitor (Figure 1E) (Zhou et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding from the study supported by data shown in Figure 1E and a citation.

claim: Treg cells and Th17 cells arise from a common progenitor.
source: Th17 cell differentiation was typically more inhibited (≥40%) than Th1, likely related to Treg cells and Th17 cells arising from a common progenitor (Figure 1E) (Zhou et al., 2008).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Unsupervised analysis revealed high similarity between artemisinin, cisapride and sertaconazole.
source: Unsupervised analysis of this phenotypic data revealed high similarity between artemisinin, cisapride and sertaconazole, including moderate enhancement of Treg cell differentiation and potent inhibition of both Th1 and Th17 cell differentiation, which may reflect effects on common pathways and direct future studies (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is a finding from computational analysis of the experimental data.

claim: The phenotypic data prioritized MBCQ, harmine, and amrinone as novel enhancers of Treg cell differentiation with favorable phenotypic profiles.
source: Importantly, these results prioritized MBCQ, harmine, and amrinone as novel enhancers of Treg cell differentiation with favorable phenotypic profiles (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and computational analysis.

claim: Sorted Treg cells generated using either Treghi or TregHAR conditions equivalently suppressed the proliferation of co-cultured responder CD4+ T cells in vitro.
source: Sorted Treg cells generated using either Treghi or TregHAR conditions equivalently suppressed the proliferation of co-cultured responder CD4+ T cells in vitro at each dilution, indicating equal efficacy between both populations of Treg cells (Figure 2A, red and blue lines).
evidence: This is a finding from in vitro suppression assays shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Treghi-Treg cells and TregHAR-Treg cells worked better than sorted tTreg cells in suppression assays, likely because they are pre-activated.
source: Both populations worked better than sorted tTreg cells, likely because they are pre-activated (Figure 2A, orange line).
evidence: This is a finding from the in vitro suppression assay with an inference about the mechanism.

claim: Antigen-specific Treg cells generated under either TregHAR or Treghi conditions caused a consistent and indistinguishable delay of onset of diabetes in the NOD-BDC2.5 model.
source: When antigen-specific Treg cells generated from NOD-BDC2.5.Foxp3IRES-GFP mice under either TregHAR or Treghi conditions were co-transferred, a consistent and indistinguishable delay of onset of diabetes was observed, with median time of diabetes onset being delayed by at least 7 days (Figure 2B, blue and red lines) (Herman et al., 2004; Tarbell et al., 2004).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo experiments shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Transfer of Treg cells generated under TregHAR conditions attenuated intestinal inflammation to a level indistinguishable from that achieved by transfer of Treghi-Treg cells in the CD45RBhi colitis model.
source: Transfer of Treg cells generated under TregHAR conditions attenuated intestinal inflammation to a level indistinguishable from that achieved by transfer of Treghi-Treg cells (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo experiments shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: Transfer of Treg cells generated under TregHAR conditions led to a comparable suppression of inflammation in a model of airway inflammation.
source: Importantly, transfer of Treg cells generated under TregHAR conditions led to a comparable suppression of inflammation (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo experiments shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Mice treated with intranasal harmine exhibited a statistically significant increase (∼20%) in the frequency of Treg cells in the draining thoracic lymph nodes compared to vehicle-treated mice.
source: Compared to mice treated only with vehicle (water), mice treated with harmine exhibited a statistically significant increase (∼20%) in the frequency of Treg cells in the draining thoracic lymph nodes; increases in absolute numbers of effector T cell subsets did not reach statistical significance (Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo experiments shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Treatment with harmine did not affect expression of Treg-relevant costimulatory molecules on dendritic cells.
source: Analyses of dendritic cell populations did not show any effect of treatment with harmine on expression of Treg-relevant costimulatory molecules, consistent with the notion that harmine predominantly acts directly on CD4+ T cells to affect Treg/Th17 differentiation in this model (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Harmine predominantly acts directly on CD4+ T cells to affect Treg/Th17 differentiation.
source: Analyses of dendritic cell populations did not show any effect of treatment with harmine on expression of Treg-relevant costimulatory molecules, consistent with the notion that harmine predominantly acts directly on CD4+ T cells to affect Treg/Th17 differentiation in this model (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the dendritic cell data.

claim: Intranasal administration of harmine during the immunization window inhibited airway inflammation at least as potently as tolerization with ovalbumin.
source: Strikingly, intranasal administration of only harmine during this window inhibited airway inflammation at least as potently as tolerization with ovalbumin (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a finding from in vivo experiments shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Harmine is a novel, potent, and specific enhancer of Treg cell differentiation with physiologically relevant effects.
source: Our results demonstrate that harmine is a novel, potent, and specific enhancer of Treg cell differentiation with physiologically relevant effects (Figures 1B, 3A).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental data shown in the figures.

claim: Harmine strongly inhibits Th17 cell differentiation.
source: In addition to its pro-Treg effect, harmine strongly inhibits Th17 cell differentiation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Even in pro-inflammatory Th17low or Th17hi conditions, harmine modestly promotes the paradoxical differentiation of Treg cells approximately twofold.
source: Notably, even in pro-inflammatory Th17low or Th17hi conditions, harmine modestly promotes the paradoxical differentiation of Treg cells approximately twofold (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At the doses used, harmine does not significantly affect culture cellularity, unlike ATRA and rapamycin.
source: At the doses used, harmine does not significantly affect culture cellularity, unlike ATRA and rapamycin (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Harmine causes a modest 24% reduction in proliferating cells at day 3 that falls to undetectable levels by day 4, less than half the reduction caused by rapamycin.
source: This observation is further substantiated by CFSE studies of cellular proliferation, which show that harmine causes a modest 24% reduction in proliferating cells at day 3 that falls to undetectable levels by day 4, less than half the reduction caused by rapamycin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from CFSE proliferation studies shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Harmine enhances absolute numbers of Treg cells to levels approaching Treghi conditions and decreases absolute numbers of Th17 cells.
source: Accordingly, harmine enhances absolute numbers of Treg cells to levels approaching Treghi conditions and decreases absolute numbers of Th17 cells (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Similar effects of harmine are observed using human CD4+ T cells, with addition of harmine potently enhancing both percentage and absolute numbers of Treg cells beyond even Treghi conditions.
source: Importantly, similar effects are observed using human CD4+ T cells, with addition of harmine potently enhancing both percentage and absolute numbers of Treg cells beyond even Treghi conditions (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding from experiments with human cells shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Addition of harmine in Th0 conditions does not skew Th differentiation towards any lineage, demonstrating that harmine's pro-Treg effect requires exogenous TGF-β1.
source: In the context of neutral Th0 conditions, addition of harmine does not skew Th differentiation towards any lineage, demonstrating that harmine's pro-Treg effect requires exogenous TGF-β1 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding from the study shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Harmine does not substitute for TGF-β1 but rather acts in conjunction with TGF-β1.
source: Thus, harmine does not substitute for TGF-β1 but rather acts in conjunction with TGF-β1.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Th0 condition experiments.

claim: Adding harmine as late as day 3 (out of 4) of culture still significantly enhances Treg cell differentiation.
source: Our results show that adding harmine as late as day 3 (out of 4) of culture still significantly enhances Treg cell differentiation (Figure 3E, top panel).
evidence: This is a finding from time-course experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Enhancement of Treg cell differentiation could be detected with as little as 4 hr of exposure to harmine.
source: The converse experiments, where culture is initiated in TregHAR conditions and harmine removed 4 hr, 1 day or 2 days later, showed complementary results. The earlier harmine was removed, the less Treg cell differentiation was enhanced, although enhancement could be detected with as little as 4 hr of exposure to harmine (Figure 3E, bottom panel).
evidence: This is a finding from time-course experiments shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The targets of harmine that impact Th differentiation are present throughout the process of differentiation.
source: These results not only reinforce the conclusion that the targets of harmine that impact Th differentiation are present throughout the process of differentiation, but also demonstrate that harmine does not impart long-lasting epigenetic signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the time-course experiments.

claim: Harmine does not impart long-lasting epigenetic signals.
source: These results not only reinforce the conclusion that the targets of harmine that impact Th differentiation are present throughout the process of differentiation, but also demonstrate that harmine does not impart long-lasting epigenetic signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the time-course experiments showing that removal of harmine reduces its effect.

claim: There is significant similarity between the expression profiles of Treghi- and TregHAR-Treg cells (Pearson correlation coefficient = 0.95).
source: These results revealed significant similarity between the expression profiles of Treghi- and TregHAR-Treg cells (Pearson correlation coefficient = 0.95, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from microarray gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: TregHAR-Treg cells showed concordant regulation of previously described canonical Treg cell signature genes.
source: As might be expected from this result, TregHAR-Treg cells showed concordant regulation of previously described canonical Treg cell signature genes (Figure 3F) (Feuerer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3F, supported by a citation.

claim: There is no evidence of significant similarity between TregHAR-Treg cells and Treg cells specialized to suppress Th1, Th2 or Th17 cells.
source: We found no evidence of significant similarity to Treg cells specialized to suppress Th1, Th2 or Th17 cells (CXCR3+, IRF4+ and GFP-FOXP3-fusion Treg cells respectively, Figure 3—figure supplement 5) (Joller et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Compared to Treghi-Treg cells, TregHAR-Treg cells showed a bias suggesting increased activation.
source: However, compared to Treghi-Treg cells, TregHAR-Treg cells showed a bias suggesting increased activation (Figure 3G) (Joller et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3G.

claim: TregHAR-Treg cells express FOXP3 at levels at least as high as, if not higher than, those of Treghi-Treg cells.
source: In addition, flow cytometry studies showed that, after gating on FOXP3+ Treg cells, TregHAR-Treg cells express FOXP3 at levels at least as high as, if not higher than, those of Treghi-Treg cells (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is a finding from flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Harmine promotes the differentiation of Treg cells that are of similar to superior function as compared to those driven by high levels of TGF-β1 alone.
source: Together, these results suggest that harmine promotes the differentiation of Treg cells that are of similar to superior function as compared to those driven by high levels of TGF-β1 alone.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gene expression and flow cytometry data.

claim: The kinetics of FOXP3 expression between Treglow, Treghi and TregHAR conditions were indistinguishable between days 0–2.
source: The kinetics of FOXP3 expression between Treglow, Treghi and TregHAR conditions were indistinguishable between days 0–2 (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is a finding from time-course flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 3I.

claim: At day 3, the percentage of FOXP3+ cells consistently decreased in Treglow conditions, while increasing identically in Treghi and TregHAR conditions.
source: At day 3, the percentage of FOXP3+ cells consistently decreased in Treglow conditions, while increasing identically in Treghi and TregHAR conditions (Figure 3I).
evidence: This is a finding from time-course flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 3I.

claim: Harmine does not enhance Treg cell differentiation by driving earlier expression of FOXP3.
source: These results argue against the notion that harmine enhances Treg cell differentiation by driving earlier expression of FOXP3.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FOXP3 kinetics data.

claim: High levels of TGF-β1 do not accelerate the early kinetics of FOXP3 expression.
source: They also suggest that high levels of TGF-β1 do not accelerate the early kinetics of FOXP3 expression, and the enhanced Treg cell differentiation seen in Treghi conditions may reflect either stabilization of the FOXP3+ state and/or higher TGF-β1 levels available at later timepoints to continue driving Treg cell differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the FOXP3 kinetics data.

claim: Only rapamycin inhibited S6-kinase phosphorylation, confirming that harmine does not inhibit mTOR activity.
source: To complement our flow cytometric studies of mTOR activity, we measured phosphorylation of another protein, S6-kinase, by Western blot. Again, only rapamycin inhibited S6-kinase phosphorylation, confirming that harmine does not inhibit mTOR activity (Figure 3J).
evidence: This is a finding from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Phosphorylation of both SMAD2 and SMAD3 was increased upon stimulation under Treglow conditions compared to naïve CD4+ T cells.
source: Phosphorylation of both SMAD2 and SMAD3 was increased upon stimulation under Treglow conditions compared to naïve CD4+ T cells, consistent with engagement of TGF-β1 signals (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is a finding from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Addition of ATRA leads to increased phosphorylation of SMAD3, but not SMAD2.
source: As previously reported, addition of ATRA leads to increased phosphorylation of SMAD3, but not SMAD2 (Figure 3K) (Xiao et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3K, supported by a citation.

claim: There was no further increase in SMAD2/3 phosphorylation upon addition of harmine, rapamycin, or TGF-β1 beyond Treglow conditions.
source: Importantly, there was no further increase in SMAD2/3 phosphorylation upon further addition of harmine, rapamycin, or TGF-β1 (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is a finding from Western blot analysis shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Harmine does not enhance Treg cell differentiation by amplifying signaling through canonical pathways (FOXP3 expression, mTOR activity, TGF-β1/SMAD signaling).
source: Taken together, these data indicate that harmine does not enhance Treg cell differentiation by amplifying signaling through these canonical pathways.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on FOXP3, mTOR, and SMAD signaling.

claim: Treghi conditions do not enhance SMAD2/3 phosphorylation beyond Treglow conditions, demonstrating that TGF-β1 itself engages pertinent and quantitative SMAD2/3-independent signals outside of tTreg cells.
source: Notably, our finding that Treghi conditions do not enhance SMAD2/3 phosphorylation beyond Treglow conditions further demonstrates that TGF-β1 itself engages pertinent and quantitative SMAD2/3-independent signals outside of tTreg cells (Figure 3K).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the Western blot data shown in Figure 3K.

claim: No difference in STAT3 phosphorylation or RORγT expression was observed when harmine was added to Th17hi conditions.
source: Kinetic analyses showed increased STAT3 phosphorylation and RORγT expression upon activation in Th17hi conditions (Figure 3L). No difference was observed when harmine was added, indicating that neither signaling event is affected by harmine (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is a finding from flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Harmine inhibits expression of Il17a, Il22, Batf, Pou2af1, and Mina in Th17 cells.
source: We verified by qPCR that harmine inhibits expression not only of the effector molecules Il17a and Il22, but also of several key regulators of the Th17 pathway, including Batf, Pou2af1 and Mina (Figure 3M) (Schraml et al., 2009; Yosef et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from qPCR analysis shown in Figure 3M, supported by citations.

claim: Harmine works on novel target(s) to modulate Treg and Th17 cell differentiation and highlights a druggable point between STAT3/RORγT signaling and other Th17 transcription factors.
source: These results suggest that harmine works on novel target(s) to modulate Treg and Th17 cell differentiation and highlight a druggable point between STAT3/RORγT signaling and other Th17 transcription factors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on Th17 pathways.

claim: A 111-gene signature was identified that was concordantly up/down-regulated in TregHAR-Treg cells vs Treghi-Treg cells, as well as in human Treg cells vs Th17 cells.
source: Since harmine also inhibits Th17 cell differentiation, we focused on a 111-gene signature that was concordantly up/down-regulated in TregHAR-Treg cells vs Treghi-Treg cells, as well as in human Treg cells vs Th17 cells (Figure 4A) (Zhang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The overlap of 16 genes between the 111-gene signature and genes in IBD-associated loci represented a significant (p < 0.01) enrichment of 1.76-fold.
source: The overlap of 16 genes represented a significant (p < 0.01) enrichment of 1.76-fold, suggesting that harmine impacts Treg cell-relevant genes implicated in IBD (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a finding from computational analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Harmine impacts Treg cell-relevant genes implicated in IBD.
source: The overlap of 16 genes represented a significant (p < 0.01) enrichment of 1.76-fold, suggesting that harmine impacts Treg cell-relevant genes implicated in IBD (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the gene overlap analysis.

claim: BACH2 is a transcription factor linked to Treg cell development and inflammation, as well as to pediatric IBD.
source: Of these, we were particularly interested in BACH2, a transcription factor linked to Treg cell development and inflammation, as well as to pediatric IBD (Christodoulou et al., 2013; Roychoudhuri et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: BACH2-deficient mice exhibit a progressive wasting disease with autoantibody formation and inflammation in the lung and gut leading to decreased survival due to defective Treg cell development and function.
source: BACH2-deficient mice exhibit a progressive wasting disease with autoantibody formation and inflammation in the lung and gut leading to decreased survival due, at least in part, to defective Treg cell development and function (Roychoudhuri et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Independent qPCR experiments confirmed differential expression of 5 of the 6 TregHAR signature genes with predicted BACH2 binding sites.
source: Independent qPCR experiments confirmed differential expression of 5 of the 6 TregHAR signature genes with predicted BACH2 binding sites, supporting the notion that harmine enhances Treg cell differentiation at least in part by modulating BACH2 signaling (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from qPCR validation shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Harmine enhances Treg cell differentiation at least in part by modulating BACH2 signaling.
source: Independent qPCR experiments confirmed differential expression of 5 of the 6 TregHAR signature genes with predicted BACH2 binding sites, supporting the notion that harmine enhances Treg cell differentiation at least in part by modulating BACH2 signaling (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the qPCR validation data.

claim: A significant number of BACH2-regulated genes are inversely regulated by harmine.
source: Intriguingly, a significant number of these BACH2-regulated genes are inversely regulated by harmine, suggesting that harmine may help reverse BACH2-axis defects, for example in IBD (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a finding from gene expression analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Harmine may help reverse BACH2-axis defects, for example in IBD.
source: Intriguingly, a significant number of these BACH2-regulated genes are inversely regulated by harmine, suggesting that harmine may help reverse BACH2-axis defects, for example in IBD (Figure 3—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the gene expression data.

claim: Harmine enhances Treg differentiation and inhibits Th17 differentiation in both wildtype and BACH2-deficient cells.
source: Importantly, harmine enhances Treg differentiation and inhibits Th17 differentiation in both wildtype and BACH2-deficient cells, indicating that harmine engages BACH2-independent programs to regulate Treg/Th17 differentiation (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from experiments with BACH2-deficient cells shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Harmine engages BACH2-independent programs to regulate Treg/Th17 differentiation.
source: Importantly, harmine enhances Treg differentiation and inhibits Th17 differentiation in both wildtype and BACH2-deficient cells, indicating that harmine engages BACH2-independent programs to regulate Treg/Th17 differentiation (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the BACH2-deficient cell experiments.

claim: Harmine does not regulate the differentiation of BACH2-deficient cells to the same level as wildtype cells, consistent with the notion that harmine also works through BACH2-dependent mechanisms.
source: Interestingly, harmine does not regulate the differentiation of BACH2-deficient cells to the same level as wildtype cells, consistent with the notion that harmine also works, at least in part, through BACH2-dependent mechanisms (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is a finding from experiments with BACH2-deficient cells shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Harmine inhibits the activity of monoamine oxidase A (MAOA), CDC-like kinases (CLKs), and dual-specificity tyrosine-phosphorylation regulated kinases (DYRKs).
source: Harmine inhibits the activity of several targets including monoamine oxidase A (MAOA), CDC-like kinases (CLKs) and dual-specificity tyrosine-phosphorylation regulated kinases (DYRKs) (Bain et al., 2007; Aranda et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inhibition of either MAOA or CLKs using moclobemide and KH-CH19, respectively, did not enhance Treg cell differentiation at any dose.
source: Inhibition of either MAOA or CLKs using moclobemide and KH-CH19, respectively, did not enhance Treg cell differentiation at any dose (Figure 4E) (Fedorov et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a finding from experiments testing different inhibitors shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Two other DYRK inhibitors, GSK-626616 and pro-INDY, similarly enhanced Treg and inhibited Th17 cell differentiation.
source: However, two other DYRK inhibitors, GSK-626616 and pro-INDY, similarly enhanced Treg and inhibited Th17 cell differentiation (Figure 4E,F) (Ogawa et al., 2010; Wippich et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding from experiments testing different DYRK inhibitors shown in Figures 4E and 4F.

claim: FACS and Western blot studies reproducibly showed higher levels of DYRK1A in Th17 than Treg cells.
source: The physiological relevance of this finding is supported by FACS and Western blot studies that reproducibly showed higher levels of DYRK1A in Th17 than Treg cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a finding from FACS and Western blot analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Non-Th17 cells generated in the context of pro-Th17 conditions do not exhibit elevated levels of DYRK1A.
source: This difference is specific; non-Th17 cells generated in the context of pro-Th17 conditions do not exhibit elevated levels of DYRK1A (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is a finding from FACS analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Knock-down of Dyrk1a in primary CD4+ T cells resulted in increased differentiation of Treg and decreased differentiation of Th17 cells.
source: Furthermore, knock-down of Dyrk1a in primary CD4+ T cells resulted in increased differentiation of Treg and decreased differentiation of Th17 cells (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is a finding from shRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4H.

claim: DYRK1A plays a central role in regulating Treg and Th17 cell differentiation.
source: Together, these data point to a central role at least for DYRK1A in regulating Treg and Th17 cell differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the DYRK inhibitor and knockdown experiments.

claim: DYRKs phosphorylate NFAT proteins, leading to their nuclear exclusion.
source: DYRKs phosphorylate several proteins (Aranda et al., 2011). Notable amongst these in the context of T cell biology are NFAT proteins, whose phosphorylation by DYRKs leads to their nuclear exclusion (Gwack et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Inhibition of DYRKs would be predicted to lead to increased levels of NFAT in the nucleus.
source: Thus, inhibition of DYRKs would be predicted to lead to increased levels of NFAT in the nucleus.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the known function of DYRKs.

claim: Nuclear translocation of NFAT1 is reproducibly enhanced approximately 40% with the addition of harmine in Treglow conditions.
source: Upon stimulation in Treglow conditions, nuclear translocation of NFAT1 is observed with an accompanying right shift of the nuclear/cytoplasmic ratio (Figure 4I, red line). This nuclear translocation of NFAT1 is reproducibly enhanced approximately 40% with the addition of harmine (Figure 4I, blue line).
evidence: This is a finding from Amnis imaging flow cytometry shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Western blot analyses showed increased NFAT1 in the nuclear compartment upon stimulation in Treglow conditions, with a similar (40%) additional increase when harmine was added.
source: In support of these results, we independently fractionated nuclei from cells treated with each of these conditions and performed Western blot analyses. These also showed increased NFAT1 in the nuclear compartment upon stimulation in Treglow conditions, with a similar (40%) additional increase when harmine was added (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is a finding from Western blot analysis of nuclear fractions shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Harmine enhances nuclear accumulation of NFAT1 at early time points up to 2 hr after stimulation.
source: Thus, harmine enhances nuclear accumulation of NFAT1 at early time points up to 2 hr after stimulation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from time-course Amnis analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: There are significant similarities in the expression profiles subsequent to either Dyrk1a knockdown or harmine treatment (Pearson correlation coefficient = 0.65).
source: RNAseq studies found significant similarities in the expression profiles subsequent to either Dyrk1a knockdown or harmine treatment (Pearson correlation coefficient = 0.65) and genes that were up- or down-regulated as a result of Dyrk1a knockdown were predominantly concordantly regulated by harmine (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, data in GSE67961).
evidence: This is a finding from RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Genes that were up- or down-regulated as a result of Dyrk1a knockdown were predominantly concordantly regulated by harmine.
source: RNAseq studies found significant similarities in the expression profiles subsequent to either Dyrk1a knockdown or harmine treatment (Pearson correlation coefficient = 0.65) and genes that were up- or down-regulated as a result of Dyrk1a knockdown were predominantly concordantly regulated by harmine (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, data in GSE67961).
evidence: This is a finding from RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Neither Dyrk1a knockdown nor harmine treatment significantly regulated genes associated with either the canonical Treg signature or the 111-gene TregHAR-Treg signature.
source: Neither Dyrk1a knockdown nor harmine treatment significantly regulated genes associated with either the canonical Treg signature or our 111-gene TregHAR-Treg signature (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Harmine does not promote Treg differentiation in the absence of TGFβ, so the differences observed in Th0 conditions may be upstream of more Treg-associated expression changes.
source: This is likely related to our observation that harmine does not promote Treg differentiation in the absence of TGFβ; the differences observed here may be upstream of more Treg-associated expression changes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the RNAseq findings based on earlier experimental observations.

claim: A relatively small number of genes (150) were differentially regulated between Dyrk1a knockdown and harmine treatment, which may reflect ancillary mechanisms engaged by harmine.
source: A relatively small number of genes (150) were differentially regulated between Dyrk1a knockdown and harmine treatment, which may in part reflect ancillary mechanisms engaged by harmine to regulate Treg/Th17 differentiation.
evidence: This is a finding from RNAseq analysis with an interpretation.

claim: DYRK1A inhibition represents a major mechanism by which harmine regulates Treg/Th17 differentiation.
source: Overall, our data are consistent with the notion that DYRK1A inhibition represents a major mechanism by which harmine regulates Treg/Th17 differentiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data on DYRK1A.

claim: Treg cells are an important regulator of immune homeostasis and an attractive therapeutic target because of their role in human inflammatory diseases such as IBD and T1D.
source: Treg cells are an important regulator of immune homeostasis and an attractive therapeutic target because of their role in human inflammatory diseases such as IBD and T1D.
evidence: This is a statement of established knowledge in the field.

claim: There remains a lack of drugs as well as druggable genes and pathways that specifically modulate Th differentiation.
source: Nevertheless, there remains a lack of drugs as well as druggable genes and pathways that specifically modulate Th differentiation.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of the field.

claim: In organ transplantation, ideal Treg cell subpopulation properties are still unclear and rapamycin is the most cutting-edge compound being used.
source: Although there is significant interest in manipulating Treg cells to treat IBD and T1D, the most mature efforts are found in the setting of organ transplantation where there is still significant room for improvement, ideal Treg cell subpopulation properties are still unclear and rapamycin is the most cutting-edge compound being used (Desreumaux et al., 2012; Long et al., 2012; Edozie et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The study's results reinforce interest in clinically used hypolipidemic statins, including lovastatin and simvastatin, as pro-Treg cell and anti-Th17 compounds.
source: In this regard, our results reinforce interest in clinically used hypolipidemic statins, including lovastatin and simvastatin, as pro-Treg cell and anti-Th17 compounds and suggest that their targets, whose geranylgeranylation are inhibited, are of fundamental and clinical interest (Kagami et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings, supported by citations.

claim: Clinical studies suggest that statins may be useful in rheumatoid arthritis, with somewhat more mixed results in systemic lupus erythematosus and multiple sclerosis.
source: Clinical studies suggest that statins may be useful in rheumatoid arthritis, with somewhat more mixed results in systemic lupus erythematosus and multiple sclerosis (Ulivieri and Baldari, 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The study's cytotoxicity data identify significant toxicity with many known Treg cell enhancers, including rapamycin.
source: Our cytotoxicity data identify significant toxicity with many known Treg cell enhancers, including rapamycin, supporting the value of a continued search.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's cytotoxicity analysis.

claim: A significant number of the Treg cell enhancers identified are antimicrobial agents, in particular antifungal agents and antimalarials.
source: Aside from the retinoic acids and statins, a significant number of them are antimicrobial agents, in particular antifungal agents (including sertaconazole, clotrimazole and pentamidine) and antimalarials (artemisinin, amodiaquine and proguanil).
evidence: This is an observation from the list of compounds identified in the study.

claim: The observation that many Treg cell enhancers are antimicrobial agents suggests how such drugs might simultaneously act on both pathogen and host.
source: This observation suggests how such drugs might simultaneously act on both pathogen and host.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the finding about antimicrobial agents.

claim: The majority of genetic polymorphisms that affect Treg cell function are unlikely to involve the few canonical genes that have been described.
source: The majority of genetic polymorphisms that affect Treg cell function are unlikely to involve the few canonical genes that have been described.
evidence: This is a statement based on inference about the genetic architecture of Treg function.

claim: Treghi conditions enhance Treg cell differentiation without increasing SMAD2 or SMAD3 phosphorylation above levels induced by Treglow conditions.
source: This is underscored by our demonstration that Treghi conditions enhance Treg cell differentiation without increasing SMAD2 or SMAD3 phosphorylation above levels induced by Treglow conditions.
evidence: This is a finding from the Western blot analysis of SMAD phosphorylation.

claim: Even the best understood Treg-relevant cytokine, TGF-β1, engages signals that remain to be fully understood.
source: Thus, even the best understood Treg-relevant cytokine, TGF-β1, engages signals that remain to be fully understood.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the SMAD phosphorylation data.

claim: ATRA can enhance Treg cell differentiation in SMAD3-deficient mice, demonstrating that ATRA's enhancement of SMAD3 signaling and Treg cell differentiation are not linked.
source: This notion is echoed by earlier discoveries that while ATRA enhances both SMAD3 signaling and Treg cell differentiation, the two are not linked as ATRA can enhance Treg cell differentiation in SMAD3-deficient mice (Nolting et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The chemical inhibitors used are significantly more specific for DYRKs as compared to other families of kinases, but their ability to distinguish between individual DYRKs is more limited.
source: While the chemical inhibitors used are significantly more specific for DYRKs as compared to other families of kinases, their ability to distinguish between individual DYRKs is more limited (Bain et al., 2007; Ogawa et al., 2010; Wippich et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature about the inhibitors.

claim: The enhanced NFAT1 nuclear translocation associated with DYRK inhibition by harmine in primary CD4+ T cells is consistent with previous studies in cell lines showing that DYRKs inhibit NFAT signaling.
source: The enhanced NFAT1 nuclear translocation we find associated with DYRK inhibition by harmine treatment in primary CD4+ T cells is consistent with previous studies in cell lines showing that DYRKs inhibit NFAT signaling (Gwack et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement connects the study's findings to prior literature.

claim: Studies showing progressively severe defects in pTreg cell generation corresponding with increasing loss of NFAT family members raise the possibility that harmine-enhanced NFAT signaling may promote Treg cell differentiation.
source: On one hand, studies showing progressively severe defects in pTreg cell generation corresponding with increasing loss of NFAT family members raise the possibility that harmine-enhanced NFAT signaling may act in the opposite manner to promote Treg cell differentiation (Vaeth et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature and involves speculation about mechanism.

claim: Decreased NFAT signaling has been reported to impair Th1 and Th17 cell differentiation.
source: However, in counterpoint to this simple association of increased NFAT with increased Treg cell differentiation, decreased NFAT signaling has also been reported to impair Th1 and Th17 cell differentiation (Ghosh et al., 2010; Hermann-Kleiter and Baier, 2010).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Patients with Down syndrome have hypofunctional Treg cells and are at increased risk for autoimmune disease.
source: Notably, patients with Down syndrome have hypofunctional Treg cells and are at increased risk for autoimmune disease (Pellegrini et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Down syndrome is characterized by trisomy of chromosome 21, and the resulting increase in DYRK1A copy number and activity is thought to be a key driver of pathology.
source: In this regard, the observation that DYRK inhibition promotes Treg cell differentiation leads to the converse prediction that increased DYRK activity would inhibit Treg cells. Down syndrome is characterized by trisomy of chromosome 21; specifically, the resulting increase in DYRK1A copy number and activity is thought to be a key driver of pathology (Lepagnol-Bestel et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Gain-of-function mutations in DYRK1B were recently implicated in metabolic syndrome.
source: Similarly, gain-of-function mutations in DYRK1B were recently implicated in metabolic syndrome (Keramati et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Decreased adipose tissue-associated Treg cells contribute to the inflammation that is a central player in obesity-induced metabolic syndrome.
source: Decreased adipose tissue-associated Treg cells contribute to the inflammation that is a central player in obesity-induced metabolic syndrome (Odegaard and Chawla, 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Increased DYRK activity in Down syndrome and metabolic syndrome patients may lead to decreased Treg cell differentiation via effects opposite to harmine's.
source: It is tempting to speculate that our findings provide a unifying hypothesis that helps account for these disparate observations, with increased DYRK activity in these patients leading to decreased Treg cell differentiation via effects opposite to harmine's.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis connecting the study's findings to human diseases.

claim: Harmine similarly enhances human Treg differentiation, supporting the likely physiologic relevance of the pathways it engages.
source: Furthermore, harmine similarly enhances human Treg differentiation, supporting the likely physiologic relevance of the pathways it engages.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the human cell experiments.

claim: DYRKs represent a novel, druggable target of particular relevance to tolerance and inflammation.
source: Taken together, we propose that DYRKs represent a novel, druggable target of particular relevance to tolerance and inflammation.
evidence: This is a concluding statement based on the study's findings.
